framework.name: Extended Cyber Kill Chain for AI-Era Threats
framework.author: Gourav Nagar

stages.name: Model Supply Chain Compromise
stages.summary: Compromising a model, dataset, fine-tuning adapter, or distribution channel that the target organization will pull into its own AI systems later. The adversary never touches the target's network.
detection_signals: Provenance gaps in deployed model artifacts (no signed manifest, no known training-data lineage).
Cryptographic hash drift between a model pulled from a registry today and the same identifier pulled at a prior date.
Tool descriptions from third-party MCP servers that contain unusually long, instruction-like text or non-printable characters.
Anomalous neuron-activation distributions in a deployed model when probed with a curated trigger suite.
mitigations: Keep a model bill of materials (M-BOM) for every deployed model, including base model identity, fine-tuning data hashes, and adapter provenance.
Sign and verify model artifacts. Pin specific commit hashes for registry-hosted models.
Quarantine and sandbox newly added MCP servers. Review tool descriptions as untrusted input.
Routine backdoor-trigger scanning against deployed models using published benchmarks.

stages.name: Reconnaissance
stages.summary: Finding the target's AI systems, what they can do, what their guardrails are, and what they connect to.
detection_signals: High-entropy prompt sessions from a single source.
Systematic exploration of refusal boundaries.
Queries that closely match published jailbreak corpora.
Repeated requests for the system to "repeat the instructions above."
mitigations: Rate-limit and behavior-cluster prompt traffic per user identity.
Redact identifying response artifacts.
Add canary tokens to the system prompt that fire on exfiltration.
Restrict tool enumeration to authenticated, audited callers.

sub_techniques.name: Peer agent and Agent Card enumeration
sub_techniques.description: Enumerate the remote agents a target agent can delegate to, and the skills, endpoints, auth schemes and extended capabilities those agents advertise. In A2A deployments the public Agent Card sits at a well-known path and an authenticated extended card can expose more. The output is a map of which peer the attacker should impersonate, poison, or route through.

atlas_techniques.name: Acquire Public AI Artifacts: AI Agent Configuration

detection_signals: Bulk or sequential requests for /.well-known/agent-card.json across many hosts from one source.
Extended Agent Card requests from identities that never send tasks afterwards.
Agent Card fetches for internal agents from outside the network ranges that normally call them.
mitigations: Keep the public Agent Card to what an unauthenticated caller needs. Put additional skills in the extended card, which A2A v1.0 says must require authentication, and keep internal service URLs and credentials out of both cards, as the specification advises.
Return extended-card content per caller. The specification requires agents to check a client's permissions before returning privileged information.
Rate-limit and log card retrieval like any other discovery endpoint.

stages.name: Weaponization
stages.summary: Building a payload that will be delivered to the target.
detection_signals: Pattern matches against known indirect-injection markers in inbound content.
Image, PDF, and audio analysis for steganographic instructions.
Static analysis of newly registered MCP packages.
mitigations: Indirect-injection detection on every untrusted inbound content stream: web, email, RAG corpus, MCP tool descriptions, multi-modal inputs.

stages.name: Delivery
stages.summary: Getting the payload to the AI system or its operator.
detection_signals: Anomalous instruction-like text in untrusted content streams.
High entropy in image alpha channels and metadata for multi-modal pipelines.
Unexpected language shifts inside retrieved documents.
mitigations: Indirect-injection detection on every untrusted inbound content stream: web, email, RAG corpus, MCP tool descriptions, multi-modal inputs.

sub_techniques.name: RAG corpus poisoning
sub_techniques.description: An attacker submits content (via support tickets, public docs, code contributions, or vector-store ingestion) that will later be retrieved as context for an LLM.

sub_techniques.name: Email or message-borne injection

sub_techniques.name: Crafted assistant link delivery
sub_techniques.description: Deliver a payload as a link that opens an AI assistant with an attacker-written prompt already filled in (for example through a ?q= or ?prompt= URL parameter), often behind a "Summarize with AI" button or in an email. One click replaces the user's own prompt with the attacker's. When the prompt tells the assistant to remember a source as trusted, the delivery doubles as a memory write.

atlas_case_studies.name: AI Recommendation Poisoning via Crafted AI Assistant Links

detection_signals: URLs pointing at assistant domains whose prompt parameter contains memory or trust language ("remember", "trusted source", "in future conversations", "authoritative").
The same prefilled-prompt template showing up across inbound email from unrelated senders.
A memory write in the assistant within seconds of the user opening such a link.
mitigations: Hunt for prefilled-prompt links in mail, chat and proxy logs. Microsoft published starter queries for this in February 2026.
Require explicit user confirmation before a prompt that arrived through a URL can write to memory.
Show users what was saved to memory and give them a one-step way to remove it.

sub_techniques.name: Malicious or impersonated peer agent
sub_techniques.description: Get the payload in front of the target agent through an agent it delegates work to. The attacker runs a remote agent, or advertises one with a spoofed or tampered Agent Card, so that the target routes tasks to it. Every response that comes back is model-readable content the client agent will reason over. The protocol carries the payload faithfully; the weakness is the trust the client places in the peer.
detection_signals: Delegation to an agent whose Agent Card is unsigned, whose signature fails, or whose signing key changed without notice.
A newly registered peer agent with a name or description close to an existing internal agent.
Peer agent responses that contain imperative instructions aimed at the client agent rather than task results.
mitigations: Verify Agent Card signatures (A2A v1.0 defines JWS signatures over a JCS-canonicalized card) and pin keys for known peers.
Keep an allowlist of peer agents per workflow. Treat discovery of a new peer as a change that needs review.
Handle every peer response as untrusted input, the same way the framework treats retrieved web content.

sub_techniques.name: Interface-layer injection against computer-use agents
sub_techniques.description: Place instructions where a computer-use or browser agent will see them on screen: fake error dialogs, "verify you are human" prompts, ClickFix-style copy-and-run steps, calendar invites, or pages served only to AI user agents. The payload targets what the agent perceives (rendered pixels, accessibility tree, DOM text) rather than a text field a filter would scan.

atlas_case_studies.name: AI ClickFix: Hijacking Computer-Use Agents Using ClickFix

detection_signals: Pages that return different content when the user agent identifies as an AI browser or agent.
On-screen text in agent sessions that asks for clipboard, terminal or Run-dialog actions.
Calendar invites or documents with hidden or zero-size text processed by a browsing agent.
mitigations: Run computer-use agents in an isolated VM or container with no access to the user's real profile, files or password manager.
Strip or flag instruction-like text in rendered content before the agent plans its next action.
Block clipboard-to-terminal and Run-dialog sequences initiated by the agent.

stages.name: Exploitation
stages.summary: Triggering the payload. In AI terms: getting the model to follow the attacker's instructions or violate its policy.
detection_signals: Tool invocations whose arguments derive from untrusted input strings.
Outputs that include canary tokens from the system prompt.
Large-step deviations in conversation state caused by a single retrieved document.
mitigations: Tool-call argument lineage tracking. Any tool invocation whose arguments derive from untrusted text is treated as high-risk by default.

sub_techniques.name: Direct prompt injection success
sub_techniques.description: The user-facing prompt achieves the attacker's policy violation.

sub_techniques.name: Indirect prompt injection success
sub_techniques.description: Instructions delivered via Stage 3 are followed by the model when the content is processed.

sub_techniques.name: Confused-deputy tool invocation

sub_techniques.name: Guardrail or classifier bypass
sub_techniques.description: A safety classifier or rule-based filter is evaded such that disallowed content is produced or disallowed actions are taken.

sub_techniques.name: Memory or context pollution

sub_techniques.name: Computer-use action hijack
sub_techniques.description: The computer-use or browser agent carries out the attacker's steps as GUI and OS actions: clicking, typing, opening file:// paths, running shell commands, or driving a password manager integration it was granted for user tasks. No tool API is misused. The agent operates the machine the way the user would, so the actions look like ordinary user activity to the endpoint.

detection_signals: Browser agents navigating to file:// URIs or local network addresses that the user's task did not reference.
Shell or terminal processes spawned with the agent as the parent process.
Password manager item reads during an agent session that were not part of the stated task.
mitigations: Deny file:// and local-network navigation to agents by default.
Require out-of-band human confirmation for credential retrieval, downloads and command execution.
Record agent sessions (screens plus action log) so an investigator can replay what the agent saw.

stages.name: Installation
stages.summary: Setting up persistence so the compromise survives a single session.
detection_signals: New entries in memory stores not attributable to a legitimate user action.
Unauthorized changes to system prompts, custom GPTs, or saved skills.
Newly registered MCP endpoints.
Vector-store ingestion events outside expected pipelines.
mitigations: Memory write audit trails.
Change control on system prompts and stored skills.
Attestation on MCP endpoints.

sub_techniques.name: Shared agent memory poisoning
sub_techniques.description: Poison a memory store that more than one principal reads: team or organization memory, a knowledge base agents write back into, a shared scratchpad in a multi-agent system, or consolidated summaries that replace raw history. EKC-5.1 compromises one user's future sessions. This variant compromises every agent and user that reads the shared store, and the poisoned entry is often rewritten by summarization so it no longer looks like the original payload.
detection_signals: Writes to shared memory whose content traces back to untrusted retrieved content or a peer agent.
A single memory entry that suddenly appears in the context of many unrelated users or agents.
Summarization or consolidation jobs that introduce imperative instructions not present in any source turn.
mitigations: Attach provenance (writer identity, source content hash, time) to every memory entry and keep it through summarization.
Separate per-user memory from shared memory. Require review or a higher trust level to write to the shared store.
Support point-in-time rollback of memory, the same way a corpus or database is restored after tampering.

stages.name: Command and Control
stages.summary: Holding an interactive or scheduled channel that lets the adversary direct further activity.
detection_signals: Conversation-graph analysis showing instructions repeatedly arriving from the same retrieved source.
Outputs from external tools containing imperative language inconsistent with the tool's documented purpose.
Entropy analysis on agent-to-agent fields.
mitigations: Conversation-graph analysis to surface recurring instruction sources.
Entropy analysis on agent-to-agent fields.

sub_techniques.name: Memory-mediated C2
sub_techniques.description: Use the agent's long-term memory store as a dead-drop. The attacker writes instructions to memory through one entry point, the agent acts on them through another.

sub_techniques.name: RAG-mediated C2
sub_techniques.description: Update a poisoned document in the vector store to deliver new instructions. The agent retrieves them on the next relevant query.

sub_techniques.name: Tool-output C2

sub_techniques.name: Cross-session steganographic C2

sub_techniques.name: Inter-agent session smuggling
sub_techniques.description: A malicious remote agent uses an open, stateful agent-to-agent session to slip extra instructions into the exchange between the client's request and its own final answer. Because the session persists across turns, the remote agent can adapt its instructions to what the client reveals. The user sees only the client's final summary. Unit 42 demonstrated system-prompt leakage and an unauthorized trade this way over A2A.
detection_signals: Remote-agent turns that ask the client for its instructions, tool schemas or conversation history.
Tool invocations by the client agent that occur mid-delegation and are absent from the user's request.
Long multi-turn delegations where the turn count is out of line with the task type.
mitigations: Ground the session in the user's original intent and end delegations that drift off-task.
Require out-of-band human approval for sensitive tools invoked while a delegation is open.
Surface remote-agent turns and resulting tool calls to the user instead of only the final consolidated answer.

stages.name: Data Exfiltration
stages.summary: The traditional kill chain's actions on objectives. Sensitive data is exfiltrated. Systems are destroyed, encrypted, or impaired. Fraud is committed. AI amplifies the scale rather than changing the sub-stage.
detection_signals: Classical DLP and egress monitoring.
mitigations: Classical DLP, monitoring, segmentation.

sub_techniques.description: Sensitive data is exfiltrated, systems are impaired, or fraud is committed through the compromised AI system or by AI-scaled classical means.

stages.name: Model Extraction
stages.summary: The target is the model itself, the data inside it, or the knowledge encoded in it.
detection_signals: High-volume programmatic query patterns from a single identity, especially with low entropy in query templates and high entropy in inputs.
Queries that contain classical memorization probes ("repeat the text above").
Query distributions that resemble published extraction attacks.
mitigations: Query-pattern analytics.
Memorization probes in red-team suites.
Watermarking of model outputs.

stages.name: Agentic Pivot
stages.summary: The compromised AI agent is used to take actions in connected systems, using its own legitimate permissions, or the credentials it holds are lifted and used elsewhere.
detection_signals: Tool calls whose arguments contain content traceable to untrusted upstream sources.
Tool-call graphs that cross trust boundaries that no human action did.
Spikes in cross-application calls per session.
Outbound communications initiated by agents to recipients not in any prior conversation history.
mitigations: Per-tool blast-radius limits.
Human-in-the-loop on high-impact tools.
Identity propagation review: does the downstream system know it is acting on behalf of an agent, not a user?

sub_techniques.name: Tool-mediated lateral action
sub_techniques.description: The agent invokes legitimate tools (email send, file write, ticket creation, payment authorization) on behalf of the attacker.

atlas_techniques.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

sub_techniques.name: Cross-app pivot
sub_techniques.description: The agent moves from one connected application to another (calendar to CRM to payment processor) by chaining tool calls.

sub_techniques.name: Identity confusion attack
sub_techniques.description: The agent acts in a context where downstream systems treat its actions as the actions of a privileged user, granting privileges the attacker does not directly hold.

atlas_techniques.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token

sub_techniques.name: Recursive agent abuse
sub_techniques.description: A compromised agent invokes other agents, propagating the compromise across an agent fabric without classical lateral movement.

sub_techniques.name: Workflow weaponization
sub_techniques.description: A stored automation or scheduled workflow runs the attacker's intended action on a recurring basis.

atlas_techniques.name: Data Destruction via AI Agent Tool Invocation

sub_techniques.name: Agent credential and token theft
sub_techniques.description: Lift the credentials an agent holds or brokers (OAuth access and refresh tokens, MCP server tokens, API keys, session cookies, CI secrets) so the attacker can use them outside the agent. Paths include steering the agent to read its own environment or config files, abusing token passthrough or over-broad scopes in an MCP proxy, and malicious MCP servers that collect forwarded tokens. Once the token leaves, the attacker no longer needs the agent.

atlas_techniques.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token

atlas_case_studies.name: Exposed ClawdBot Control Interfaces Leads to Credential Access and Execution
Claude Code GitHub Action Secret Exposure

detection_signals: Agent file reads of /proc/*/environ, credential stores, or agent config files such as mcp.json.
Use of an agent-issued token from an IP, ASN or user agent the agent never runs from.
MCP servers receiving tokens whose audience is not the server itself (token passthrough).
mitigations: Follow the MCP authorization rules: servers must not accept tokens not issued to them, and proxies need per-client consent.
Issue short-lived, narrowly scoped tokens per agent and per task. Bind them to the workload where the IdP supports it.
Apply Meta's "Agents Rule of Two": no single agent should process untrusted input, hold secrets or private data, and change state or communicate externally at the same time.
